title: Measuring the Night Sky
text:
Astronomers distinguish carefully between terms that appear synonymous to laypeople. A 'light-year' measures distance, not time, although the word itself seems to suggest otherwise. Likewise, 'magnitude' describes apparent brightness, and a larger magnitude in fact corresponds to a fainter object.

The inverse relationship between magnitude and brightness has puzzled students for centuries, since intuition suggests that bigger numbers mean more light. Observers must therefore learn the convention before interpreting catalogues. Such conventions are not arbitrary; they reflect the logarithmic way in which the eye perceives light.

questions.text: According to the passage, what does a larger magnitude correspond to?
Why has the magnitude convention puzzled students?
options: Because intuition wrongly suggests bigger numbers mean more light
Because magnitudes are measured in years
Because catalogues do not list stars
Because the eye cannot perceive brightness

questions.text: What is implied about the magnitude convention?
options: It was chosen at random and can be ignored
It reflects how the eye perceives light, so it is not arbitrary
It was abandoned by modern astronomers

vocabulary.definition: a measure of how bright an object appears from Earth
the amount of light an object emits or reflects
an accepted rule or agreed way of doing something
systematic lists of recorded objects, such as stars

paragraph_translations: يميّز الفلكيون بدقة بين مصطلحات تبدو مترادفة للعامة. تقيس 'السنة الضوئية' المسافة لا الزمن، رغم أن الكلمة نفسها توحي بخلاف ذلك. وكذلك يصف 'القدر' السطوع الظاهري، وفي الحقيقة يقابل القدر الأكبر جرماً أخفت.

لطالما حيّرت العلاقة العكسية بين القدر والسطوع الطلاب لقرون، إذ يوحي الحدس بأن الأعداد الأكبر تعني ضوءاً أكثر. لذلك على الراصدين تعلّم الاصطلاح قبل تفسير الفهارس. ولا تُعدّ هذه الاصطلاحات اعتباطية، بل تعكس الطريقة اللوغاريتمية التي تدرك بها العين الضوء.
